newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO sidesteps war crimes role in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: NATO sidesteps war crimes role in Bosnia.

text.p: NATO has carefully sidestepped the task of arresting Bosnia's indicted war criminals but critics say its intelligence network and elite troops are perfectly suited for the job.

U.S. military officials this week started promoting the idea of a separate international police force to hunt war crimes suspects, saying the NATO-led peace force in Bosnia was not trained for "police work".

The proposal was still vague but defence officials said on Wednesday the police force might operate under the European Union, the U.N. war crimes tribunal or the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
Balkan commentators said none of those organisations had the means or the experience to track down suspects in a former war zone, some of whom travel under heavy guard.
"They have no experience in this kind of thing. Who are they going to hire?" said Chris Bennett of the International Crisis Group, a private agency monitoring the peace process.
"It would be a force of bounty hunters and out-of-work cops."
NATO should employ its elaborate intelligence resources and call upon special units among alliance members, including Britain's elite SAS regiment, Bennett told Reuters in Sarajevo.
He said discussion of a new police force was meant to distract attention from the West's reluctance to go after war crimes suspects still at large.

"NATO is clearly trying to find a way of shirking its obligations in this country," he said. "The onus is on NATO here. It's irresponsible to be talking about setting up police forces and it's cowardly."

The alliance has come under criticism for refusing to unleash its peacekeeping force to hunt down those charged by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, including former Serb wartime leader Radovan Karadzic and army commander Ratko Mladic.
Official NATO policy says troops will not launch "manhunts" but will arrest suspects encountered during the course of normal duties if the "situation permits".

Privately, NATO officers say arresting war crimes suspects would risk casualties and a possible backlash from local armies and police against peacekeeping troops, unarmed international police monitors and aid workers.
Rival armies have mostly cooperated with the peace treaty and NATO officers say arresting war crimes suspects could jeopardise that cooperation.
The international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, has called on Western powers to send specially-trained units but has never mentioned forming a "police" force.
Bildt and tribunal prosecutors say there will be no genuine reconciliation and lasting peace in Bosnia if indicted war criminals are allowed to go free.
Britain and France have been reluctant to push for the arrest of war crimes suspects and have yet to comment on the suggested police force.
Michael Williams, of the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said the proposal could be an empty U.S. gesture aimed at deflecting criticism.
"It's another way for the Clinton administration to get off the hook on the war crimes issue," Williams said by telephone.
